write.desc: This topic covers series whose terms change sign. Its points belong together because they all turn on the gap between absolute and conditional convergence: the tests that prove convergence (ratio, root, Leibniz), how to choose and justify a test, and why only absolute convergence lets a series be rearranged and multiplied like a finite sum.

points.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence
points.what: The learner can define absolute and conditional convergence and prove that if the sum of |a_n| converges then the sum of a_n converges, using the Cauchy criterion for series and the triangle inequality.
outside: Cauchy criterion for convergence of series

points.name: Alternating series (Leibniz) test
points.what: The learner can state the test (terms alternate in sign, decrease in absolute value and tend to zero) and prove it, either by showing the even and odd partial sums are monotone and squeeze together or through the Cauchy criterion.
outside: convergence of a sequence whose even and odd subsequences converge to the same limit

points.name: Error bound for alternating series
points.what: The learner can prove that for a Leibniz series the sum lies between consecutive partial sums, so |S - s_n| <= a_{n+1}, and use this to estimate a sum to a given accuracy.

points.name: Conditional convergence: the alternating harmonic series
points.what: The learner can show that the alternating harmonic series converges but not absolutely, which proves that convergence does not imply absolute convergence, and can recognise other conditionally convergent series.

points.name: The ratio test
points.what: The learner can state the ratio test with limsup and liminf of |a_{n+1}/a_n|, prove absolute convergence when the limsup is below 1 by comparison with a geometric series, and prove divergence when the liminf is above 1 (or the ratio is eventually at least 1) because the terms do not tend to zero.
outside: limsup and liminf of a sequence
comparison test for series with nonnegative terms

points.name: The root test
points.what: The learner can state the root test with L = limsup |a_n|^(1/n) and prove absolute convergence when L < 1 by comparison with a geometric series, and divergence when L > 1 because |a_n| > 1 infinitely often.
outside: limsup and liminf of a sequence
comparison test for series with nonnegative terms

points.name: Comparing the ratio and root tests and the inconclusive case
points.what: The learner can show with p-series that a limit of 1 in either test decides nothing, prove the inequalities liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| <= liminf |a_n|^(1/n) <= limsup |a_n|^(1/n) <= limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|, conclude that the root test is at least as strong as the ratio test, and give a series where the root test works but the ratio test fails.
outside: convergence of p-series exactly when p > 1

points.name: Choosing a test for a given series
points.what: The learner can look at a series, pick a suitable test (term test, comparison, ratio, root, Leibniz, absolute convergence first) for reasons they can state, and write the argument as a complete proof that checks every hypothesis.

points.name: Positive and negative parts of a series
points.what: The learner can split a series into its positive and negative parts and prove that it converges absolutely exactly when both parts converge, while for a conditionally convergent series both parts diverge to infinity.
outside: series with nonnegative terms converge exactly when their partial sums are bounded

points.name: Rearranging an absolutely convergent series
points.what: The learner can define a rearrangement as a bijection of the indices and prove that every rearrangement of an absolutely convergent series converges to the same sum.
outside: Cauchy criterion for convergence of series

points.name: The Riemann rearrangement theorem
points.what: The learner can explain, and sketch the proof, that a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any real number or to diverge, by taking positive terms until the target is passed and then negative terms, and can see a concrete rearrangement of the alternating harmonic series with a different sum.

points.name: The Cauchy product and Mertens' theorem
points.what: The learner can define the Cauchy product of two series, prove that the product of two absolutely convergent series converges absolutely to the product of their sums, and state Mertens' theorem that one absolutely convergent factor is enough.

points.name: A Cauchy product that diverges
points.what: The learner can show that the Cauchy product of the convergent series sum (-1)^n / sqrt(n+1) with itself diverges because its terms do not tend to zero, so conditional convergence of both factors is not enough.

points.name: Dirichlet's and Abel's tests (optional)
points.what: The learner can use summation by parts to prove Dirichlet's test (bounded partial sums times a sequence decreasing to zero) and Abel's test, and see the Leibniz test as a special case.
outside: Cauchy criterion for convergence of series

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Section 2.7 Properties of Infinite Series (absolute convergence, alternating series test, rearrangements); Section 2.1 on rearrangements; Section 2.8 Double Summations and Products of Infinite Series

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis (4th ed.)
